articles.title: Scientists trace mysterious radio signals to a dead star 5,000 light-years away
articles.description: THE TAKEAWAYS: Researchers discovered a mysterious star system that emits radio signals every eight minutes. One of the stars is a white dwarf. The other is a G-type star which is similar to the Sun. These star systems belong to a group known as long-period transients, which produce radio signals that turn on and off. A group of researchers has discovered a mysterious star system more than 5,000 light-years away that emits radio signals every eight minutes. Scientists Discover Massive Dwarf Planet Lurking In The Outer Solar System Scientists at Curtin University's node of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) in Perth, Australia, have linked the rare radio pulses to an unusual star system known as GPM J071507−114153. The system consists of two stars orbiting each other: a dead star that spins every eight minutes and another star similar to our own Sun. One of the stars is a white dwarf, the dense core left behind when a star dies. The other is a G-type star, a classification that includes our own Sun. End Of An Era As Nasa Telescope That Detected Thousands Of Gamma-ray Bursts Nears Its Final Days "We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, a co-author of the paper, said. The team analyzed more than 100 hours of radio data to better understand the movement of the white dwarf. "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," lead author and Square Kilometre Array Observatory commissioning scientist Dr. Sam McSweeney said. Typically, these types of radio signals have been detected coming from systems containing smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. However, this newly discovered system is different because it includes a star similar to our own Sun, making it a rare find. How To Watch Fox Weather "It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away," Associate Professor Hurley-Walker said. These star systems belong to a group known as long-period transients (LPTs), which produce radio signals that turn on and off at intervals ranging from a few minutes to several hours. Since the first LPT system was discovered in 2021, astronomers have identified only about a dozen others. Nasa Launches Spacex’s Crew-13 On A Record-breaking Journey To The International Space Station While several previously discovered systems also contain a white dwarf paired with another star, scientists have not been able to determine which star is responsible for producing the unusual radio signals. "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find," Associate Professor Hurley-Walker said. Original article source: Scientists discover star system sending strange radio signals every eight minutes from deep space This article originally appeared on Fox Weather at https://www.foxweather.com/earth-space/scientists-discover-star-system-sending-strange-signals-every-eight-minutes

articles.description: A recent reanalysis of the outsize black hole galaxy UHZ1 using existing X-ray data and new infrared observations challenges a previous groundbreaking claim. Three years ago, this galaxy made news for hosting an unusually massive and heavily dust-obscured black hole formed through direct collapse. Led by Fan Zou of the University of Michigan, the new study reports no signs of hidden black hole activity. The paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal on Oct. 14, suggests UHZ1 could be a low-mass, metal-poor, star-forming galaxy.

articles.title: Why Skydio Built a Lopsided Drone
articles.description: Skydio’s drones have always been magical. From MIT research and early prototypes to what I would argue is still the most advanced consumer drone ever made, this is a company that makes very cool stuff. Sadly, Skydio no longer makes cool stuff for consumers, instead focusing on drone platforms for public safety, inspection, and other things that, on a good day, don’t affect me personally. Even so, a new drone from Skydio is worth paying attention to, especially when it’s as weird as this one—the F10 Lightrunner is a fixed-wing camera drone designed for autonomous deployment and high-speed flight, all while looking so lopsided that it’s surprising that it can actually fly. The benefits of asymmetrical aircraft There’s a short rabbit hole you can go down if you start looking for other examples of asymmetrical aircraft. In the 1990s, legendary aircraft designer Burt Rutan and his company Scaled Composites built some decidedly odd airplanes, including the Model 202 Boomerang. But perhaps the most famous asymmetrical aircraft was the Blohm & Voss BV 141, a World War 2-era reconnaissance plane that featured an engine in the middle alongside a crew compartment alarmingly offset out onto the right wing. The unique design was intended to give the crew the best possible view for reconnaissance missions, because in a typical single-engine aircraft, the crew sits right behind the engine, limiting forward visibility. Nearly 90 years later, the Skydio F10 is applying a similar philosophy to fixed-wing reconnaissance drones, which typically track targets by flying around them in circles. “While turning at low altitudes, it becomes very hard to avoid occluding a camera with a wing or a tail,” explains Andrew Goessling, director of engineering at Skydio. “So we were analyzing a lot of these use cases, and one of our engineers just blurted out, ‘what if we put the camera on the wingtip?’ And that’s where it all started, because as long as you only turn left, a lot of these problems just go away.” Of course, putting the camera on the F10’s wingtip creates a bunch of new problems, chief among them that the aircraft is no longer balanced. Not only is the camera payload fairly heavy relative to the total mass of the drone, but its bulk also creates greater drag. This is why the seemingly straightforward solution of putting something else (like a battery) on the other wingtip to rebalance the drone isn’t practical, says Goessling. “The issue there is that the camera represents a substantial portion of the total aircraft drag, so putting something else on the other wing would cut your flight time nearly in half.” Goessling points out that there’s nothing inherently bad about an asymmetric design like the F10; it just makes the life of engineers either a little more difficult or a little more exciting, depending on your perspective. “There were really two challenges here: What is the optimal design for an aircraft with a wingtip camera, and then once you have the design, how are you going to control it?” Any fixed-wing aircraft design has to consider three factors: distribution of mass, how thrust is distributed between the motors, and how the shape and location of the wings affect the aircraft’s aerodynamics. Once Skydio decided on their requirements for the F10—including the wingtip camera, two motors to enable controllable hovering for takeoff and landing, and a high top speed and long flight time—the engineers used a modeling and optimization approach to explore design options. The resulting aircraft compensates for the wing-mounted camera payload by extending just that wing to provide more lift on that side, and repositioning the motors asymmetrically to balance thrust against the added drag of the camera. Maneuvering with MegaDock An added challenge was getting the F10 to launch and recover with a robot arm, using a storage, charging, and deployment system called the MegaDock. That requires the drone to transition from hover to forward flight and then back again—a particularly difficult trick for a flying wing with no tail control surfaces (movable parts of the wing used to steer the aircraft). The F10 uses model predictive control (a control technique based on a detailed physics model of the robot) to accomplish this autonomously, and a single control policy can handle the robot all the way through its entire flight envelope, from a stationary hover to its maximum flight speed of 100 miles per hour. In other words, there’s no “hover mode” or “flight mode,” so the mission planner just tells the drone where it needs to be, and the drone will know how to get itself there. In operation, Skydio’s MegaDock can handle up to five F10s, allowing for continuous flight operations with three drones while two recharge. The entire system is fully autonomous, with humans only needed for remote supervisory control, communicating with the F10 via dual 5G cellular modems. Maximum flight time is two hours, and the aircraft is equipped with the same kind of magical obstacle-dodging camera setup as Skydio’s quadrotor drones. If something goes seriously wrong, an integrated parachute in the F10’s butt will deploy, lowering the drone to the ground gently enough that it’s safe to fly over people. Goessling is the first to acknowledge that the F10 Lightrunner is an unconventional design, but he’s proud of what he and his team have come up with as a commercially viable solution to the occlusion issue with other fixed-wing drones. “It looks weird, and we got some pushback from some of the less technical parts of the company,” Goessling says. “If there were less crazy ways of doing it, we would have pursued them. But we have the data. We have sound reasons for every decision we’ve made. And the outcome at the end was well worth it.”

articles.title: To watch and watch for: Week of Nov. 15
articles.description: Fall recess is approaching, and whether or not you're celebrating Thanksgiving, the days off will be a much appreciated break from all our academic and professional obligations. If you find yourself looking for activities to fill the time, we've got plenty of recommendations for you. From novels to films to music, we have a wide range of selections to point you towards. We also have events for this week and the next - in case you're in Baltimore for the break! This year's Anora may be Jordan Firstman's Club Kid: an indie festival hit that has its theatrical release during break. The film follows Peter (Jordan Firstman), a New York club promoter with an accordingly whirlwind party-goer lifestyle, who deals with the sudden arrival of a ten-year-old kid he never knew he had. As he adjusts to newfound fatherhood, he also deals with the need to re-evaluate what his life should really entail. Club Kid and its understated but sincere charm will be the perfect watch for the Thanksgiving season as it questions what truly makes a family. The New York Times bestselling author T.J. Klune's newest mystery romance, Murmuration, will be a great cozy read. The novel is set in a seemingly idyllic small town that begins to slowly grow more odd. Mike, the protagonist, works his dream job at the local bookstore. He's ready to take the next step in his burgeoning romance with the small diner's waiter before he realizes the town they live in isn't quite what it seems. Murmuration's mystery will surely captivate any reader. The hotly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI releases on Friday, so maybe you're ready to spend the rest of your break with the video game of the year. Even if you're not a Grand Theft Auto fan, the game's accompanying album features new songs from some of the best working musical artists today. Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album already has singles from Young Lean, Metro Boomin, Future, Travis Scott, Morgan Wallen and Cardi B released ahead of the full album. PinkPantheress, Tame Impala and SZA are some of the other artists credited to appear on the tracklist. Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album's vast artist ensemble ensures that it will have something for everyone. During the upcoming break, the critically acclaimed The Wild Robot will be screening for free at The Walters Art Museum on Sunday, Nov. 22! The Wild Robot was nominated for the Best Animated Feature at the 2024 Academy Awards and it was widely praised in that year's award season. The film follows a sentient robot named Roz after she is shipwrecked and stranded on an island. Luckily, she manages to find a community in her harsh, unknown environment. The Wild Robot is a story about the importance of harmony with nature and those around you, and it makes for a moving watch this Thanksgiving season. As always, if you're looking for more activities to fill your time, we have a full list below: To watch… Club Kid, directed by Jordan Firstman - Nov. 26 All of a Sudden, directed by Ryusuke Hamaguchi - Nov. 25 Paper Tiger, directed by James Gray- Nov. 20 Minotaur, directed by Andrey Zvyagintsev - Nov. 20 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, directed by Francis Lawrence- Nov. 20 To read… Murmuration, written by T.J. Klune - Nov. 17 Tiger's Mouth, written by Lucy Tan - Nov. 17 Nanny Nanny, written by K. Chiucarello - Nov. 17 Universe of Grace, written by Rachel Calnek-Sugin - Nov. 17 Deadlock, written by Chloe Gong - Nov. 17 To listen… Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, by Various Artists - Nov. 19 Stargazer, by cikho - Nov. 20 Act 2, by Mother Soki - Nov. 20 Cute & Anxiety, by Yves - Nov. 20 SUIATSU, by Stray Kids - Nov. 25 Live Events… Sunday Screening: The Wild Robot - Nov. 22, 2-4 p.m. at The Walters Art Museum Registration is free and required.
